source_note: Evidence excerpts are MITRE ATT&CK procedure summaries. Publication links identify cited references; the original vendor reports were not downloaded.

ref-099b182b87d642313f3a.text: SUNBURST communicated via HTTP GET or HTTP POST requests to third party servers for C2. SUNBURST masqueraded its network traffic as the Orion Improvement Program (OIP) protocol. SUNBURST delivered different payloads, including TEARDROP in at least one instance. SUNBURST used DNS for C2 traffic designed to mimic normal SolarWinds API communications. SUNBURST was digitally signed by SolarWinds from March - May 2020. SUNBURST collected information from a compromised host. SUNBURST obfuscated collected system information using a FNV-1a + XOR algorithm. SUNBURST collected device `UPTIME`. SUNBURST collected the username from a compromised host. SUNBURST remained dormant after initial access for a period of up to two weeks. SUNBURST collected a list of process names that were hashed using a FNV-1a + XOR algorithm to check against similarly-hashed hardcoded blocklists. SUNBURST had commands that allow an attacker to write or delete registry keys, and was observed stopping services by setting their HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\services\\[service_name]\\Start registry entries to value 4. It also deleted previously-created Image File Execution Options (IFEO) Debugger registry values and registry keys related to HTTP proxy to clean up traces of its activity. SUNBURST used the WMI query Select * From Win32_SystemDriver to retrieve a driver listing. SUNBURST collected hostname and OS version. TEARDROP files had names that resembled legitimate Window file and directory names. TEARDROP checked that HKU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\CTF existed before decoding its embedded payload. SUNBURST collected the registry value HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGuid from compromised hosts. SUNBURST had a command to delete files. SUNBURST dynamically resolved C2 infrastructure for randomly-generated subdomains within a parent domain. SUNBURST used Base64 encoding in its C2 traffic. SUNBURST collected a list of service names that were hashed using a FNV-1a + XOR algorithm to check against similarly-hashed hardcoded blocklists. SUNBURST had commands to enumerate files and directories. SUNBURST collected all network interface MAC addresses that are up and not loopback devices, as well as IP address, DHCP configuration, and domain information. SUNBURST added junk bytes to its C2 over HTTP. SUNBURST encrypted C2 traffic using a single-byte-XOR cipher.
ref-099b182b87d642313f3a.title: FireEye. (2020, December 13). Highly Evasive Attacker Leverages SolarWinds Supply Chain to Compromise Multiple Global Victims With SUNBURST Backdoor. Retrieved January 4, 2021.

ref-1fb4e562aa108937ccb6.text:
ComRAT has injected its orchestrator DLL into explorer.exe. ComRAT has also injected its communications module into the victim's default browser to make C2 connections appear less suspicious as all network connections will be initiated by the browser process.
ComRAT has encrypted its virtual file system using AES-256 in XTS mode.
ComRAT has checked the victim system's date and time to perform tasks during business hours (9 to 5, Monday to Friday).
ComRAT has the ability to use the Gmail web UI to receive commands and exfiltrate information.
ComRAT has modified Registry values to store encrypted orchestrator code and payloads.
ComRAT has used PowerShell to load itself every time a user logs in to the system. ComRAT can execute PowerShell scripts loaded into memory or from the file system.
ComRAT has stored encrypted orchestrator code and payloads in the Registry.
ComRAT can use SSL/TLS encryption for its HTTP-based C2 channel. ComRAT has used public key cryptography with RSA and AES encrypted email attachments for its Gmail C2 channel.
ComRAT has embedded a XOR encrypted communications module inside the orchestrator module.
ComRAT has used encryption and base64 to obfuscate its orchestrator code in the Registry. ComRAT has also used encoded PowerShell scripts.
ComRAT has used unique per machine passwords to decrypt the orchestrator payload and a hardcoded XOR key to decrypt its communications module. ComRAT has also used a unique password to decrypt the file used for its hidden file system.
ComRAT has used a scheduled task to launch its PowerShell loader.
ref-1fb4e562aa108937ccb6.title: CISA. (2020, October 29). Malware Analysis Report (AR20-303A). Retrieved December 9, 2020.

ref-26fc1e5708187458bc77.text: Ryuk has injected itself into remote processes to encrypt files using a combination of VirtualAlloc, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread. Ryuk has called GetLogicalDrives to emumerate all mounted drives, and GetDriveTypeW to determine the drive type. Ryuk has enumerated files and folders on all mounted drives. Ryuk has called CreateToolhelp32Snapshot to enumerate all running processes. Ryuk has used the Windows command line to create a Registry entry under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to establish persistence. Ryuk has attempted to adjust its token privileges to have the SeDebugPrivilege. Ryuk has called kill.bat for stopping services, disabling services and killing processes. Ryuk has used cmd.exe to create a Registry entry to establish persistence. Ryuk has used multiple native APIs including ShellExecuteW to run executables,GetWindowsDirectoryW to create folders, and VirtualAlloc, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread for process injection. Ryuk has constructed legitimate appearing installation folder paths by calling GetWindowsDirectoryW and then inserting a null byte at the fourth character of the path. For Windows Vista or higher, the path would appear as C:\Users\Public. Ryuk has been observed to query the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Nls\Language and the value InstallLanguage. If the machine has the value 0x419 (Russian), 0x422 (Ukrainian), or 0x423 (Belarusian), it stops execution. Ryuk has used a combination of symmetric (AES) and asymmetric (RSA) encryption to encrypt files. Files have been encrypted with their own AES key and given a file extension of .RYK. Encrypted directories have had a ransom note of RyukReadMe.txt written to the directory. Ryuk has used vssadmin Delete Shadows /all /quiet to to delete volume shadow copies and vssadmin resize shadowstorage to force deletion of shadow copies created by third-party applications.
ref-26fc1e5708187458bc77.title: Hanel, A. (2019, January 10). Big Game Hunting with Ryuk: Another Lucrative Targeted Ransomware. Retrieved May 12, 2020.

ref-2e5ce0b63b29a50bf2af.text: Raspberry Robin uses rundll32 execution without any command line parameters to contact command and control infrastructure, such as IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin retrieves its second stage payload in a variety of ways such as through msiexec.exe abuse, or running the curl command to download the payload to the victim's %AppData% folder. Raspberry Robin uses newly-registered domains containing only a few characters for command and controll purposes, such as "v0[.]cx". Raspberry Robin uses regsvr32.exe execution without any command line parameters for command and control requests to IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin uses mixed-case letters for filenames and commands to evade detection. Raspberry Robin uses msiexec.exe for post-installation communication to command and control infrastructure. Msiexec.exe is executed referencing a remote resource for second-stage payload retrieval and execution. Raspberry Robin uses the Windows utility odbcconf.exe to execute malicious commands, using the regsvr flag to execute DLLs and bypass application control mechanisms that are not monitoring for odbcconf.exe abuse. Raspberry Robin is capable of contacting the TOR network for delivering second-stage payloads. Raspberry Robin has historically been delivered via infected USB drives containing a malicious LNK object masquerading as a legitimate folder. Raspberry Robin uses cmd.exe to read and execute a file stored on an infected USB device as part of initial installation. Raspberry Robin will communicate via HTTP over port 8080 for command and control traffic. Raspberry Robin uses outbound HTTP requests containing victim information for retrieving second stage payloads. Variants of Raspberry Robin can download archive files (such as 7-Zip files) via the victim web browser for second stage execution. Raspberry Robin has historically used infected USB media to spread to new victims. Raspberry Robin will use the legitimate Windows utility fodhelper.exe to run processes at elevated privileges without requiring a User Account Control prompt.
ref-2e5ce0b63b29a50bf2af.title: Lauren Podber and Stef Rand. (2022, May 5). Raspberry Robin gets the worm early. Retrieved May 17, 2024.

ref-5d0ba45f8d6cd90287bf.text: ThiefQuest uses a function named is_debugging to perform anti-debugging logic. The function invokes sysctl checking the returned value of P_TRACED. ThiefQuest also calls ptrace with the PTRACE_DENY_ATTACH flag to prevent debugging. ThiefQuest uses various API functions such as NSCreateObjectFileImageFromMemory to load and link in-memory payloads. ThiefQuest can download and execute payloads in-memory or from disk. ThiefQuest encrypts a set of file extensions on a host, deletes the original files, and provides a ransom note with no contact information. ThiefQuest uses various API to perform behaviors such as executing payloads and performing local enumeration.
ref-5d0ba45f8d6cd90287bf.title: Patrick Wardle. (2020, July 3). OSX.EvilQuest Uncovered part ii: insidious capabilities. Retrieved March 21, 2021.

ref-65970019fd9baa05199d.text:
LockBit 2.0 will not execute on hosts where the system language is set to a language spoken in the Commonwealth of Independent States region.
LockBit 2.0 can delete log files through the use of wevtutil.
LockBit 2.0 can enumerate local drive configuration.
LockBit 2.0 can enumerate system information including hostname and domain information.
LockBit 2.0 can be executed via scheduled task.
LockBit 2.0 can check if a targeted machine is using a set of Eastern European languages and exit without infection if so.
LockBit 2.0 can decode scripts and strings in loaded modules.
LockBit 2.0 can execute command line arguments in a hidden window.
LockBit 2.0 can bypass UAC through creating the Registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ICM\Calibration`.
LockBit 2.0 has been observed creating accounts for persistence using simple names like "a".
LockBit 2.0 can delete itself from disk after execution.
LockBit 2.0 can disable firewall rules and anti-malware and monitoring software including Windows Defender.
LockBit 2.0 can use the PowerShell module `InvokeGPUpdate` to modify Group Policy.
LockBit 2.0 has the ability to move laterally via SMB.
LockBit 2.0 can modify Group Policy to disable Windows Defender and to automatically infect devices in Windows domains.
LockBit 2.0 can use the Windows command shell for multiple post-compromise actions on objective.
LockBit 2.0 can use standard AES and elliptic-curve cryptography algorithms to encrypt victim data.
ref-65970019fd9baa05199d.title: Elsad, A. et al. (2022, June 9). LockBit 2.0: How This RaaS Operates and How to Protect Against It. Retrieved January 24, 2025.

ref-731c1764a706b3b574e0.text:
Raccoon Stealer queries the Windows Registry to fingerprint the infected host via the `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGuid` key.
Raccoon Stealer gathers information on the infected system owner and user.
Raccoon Stealer is capable of identifying running software on victim machines.
Raccoon Stealer can remove files related to use and installation.
Raccoon Stealer collects files and directories from victim systems based on configuration data downloaded from command and control servers.
Raccoon Stealer uses RC4 encryption for strings and command and control addresses to evade static detection.
Raccoon Stealer uses RC4-encrypted, base64-encoded strings to obfuscate functionality and command and control servers.
Raccoon Stealer dynamically links key WinApi functions during execution.
Raccoon Stealer will automatically collect and exfiltrate data identified in received configuration files from command and control nodes.
Raccoon Stealer uses HTTP, and particularly HTTP POST requests, for command and control actions.
Raccoon Stealer uses existing HTTP-based command and control channels for exfiltration.
ref-731c1764a706b3b574e0.title: Quentin Bourgue, Pierre le Bourhis, & Sekoia TDR. (2022, June 28). Raccoon Stealer v2 - Part 1: The return of the dead. Retrieved August 1, 2024.

ref-8078a6bdb34a10246c85.text: Cobalt Strike can conduct peer-to-peer communication over Windows named pipes encapsulated in the SMB protocol. All protocols use their standard assigned ports. Cobalt Strike has the ability to use an Excel Workbook to execute additional code by enabling Office to trust macros and execute code without user permission. Cobalt Strike can use self signed Java applets to execute signed applet attacks. Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload can collect information on process details. Cobalt Strike uses the native Windows Network Enumeration APIs to interrogate and discover targets in a Windows Active Directory network. Cobalt Strike has the ability to use AES-256 symmetric encryption in CBC mode with HMAC-SHA-256 to encrypt task commands and XOR to encrypt shell code and configuration data. Cobalt Strike can query HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\\Excel\Security\AccessVBOM\ to determine if the security setting for restricting default programmatic access is enabled. Cobalt Strike can perform port scans from an infected host. Cobalt Strike has the ability to load DLLs via reflective injection. Cobalt Strike can exploit Oracle Java vulnerabilities for execution, including CVE-2011-3544, CVE-2013-2465, CVE-2012-4681, and CVE-2013-2460. Cobalt Strike can produce a sessions report from compromised hosts. Cobalt Strike can hash functions to obfuscate calls to the Windows API and use a public/private key pair to encrypt Beacon session metadata. Cobalt Strike uses a command-line interface to interact with systems. The Cobalt Strike System Profiler can use JavaScript to perform reconnaissance actions. Cobalt Strike can deliver additional payloads to victim machines. Cobalt Strike can use RSA asymmetric encryption with PKCS1 padding to encrypt data sent to the C2 server. Cobalt Strike can be configured to use TCP, ICMP, and UDP for C2 communications. Cobalt Strike can use a custom command and control protocol that can be encapsulated in DNS. All protocols use their standard assigned ports. Cobalt Strike can modify Registry values within HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\\Excel\Security\AccessVBOM\ to enable the execution of additional code. Cobalt Strike can download a hosted "beacon" payload using BITSAdmin. Cobalt Strike has the ability to use Smart Applet attacks to disable the Java SecurityManager sandbox.
ref-8078a6bdb34a10246c85.title: Mavis, N. (2020, September 21). The Art and Science of Detecting Cobalt Strike. Retrieved September 12, 2024.

ref-9a160e23c7da35c0f4d7.text: Stuxnet attempts to impersonate an anonymous token to enumerate bindings in the service control manager. Stuxnet uses encrypted configuration blocks and writes encrypted files to disk. Stuxnet transforms encrypted binary data into an ASCII string in order to use it as a URL parameter value. Stuxnet encodes the payload of system information sent to the command and control servers using a one byte 0xFF XOR key. Stuxnet also uses a 31-byte long static byte string to XOR data sent to command and control servers. The servers use a different static key to encrypt replies to the implant. Stuxnet enumerates user accounts of the local host. Stuxnet collects the IP address of a compromised system. Stuxnet uses a driver registered as a boot start service as the main load-point. Stuxnet calls LoadLibrary then executes exports from a DLL. Stuxnet infects remote servers via network shares and by infecting WinCC database views with malicious code. Stuxnet uses the SetSecurityDescriptorDacl API to reduce object integrity levels. Stuxnet enumerates the directories of a network resource. Stuxnet used MS10-073 and an undisclosed Task Scheduler vulnerability to escalate privileges on local Windows machines. Stuxnet can propagate via peer-to-peer communication and updates using RPC. Stuxnet used xp_cmdshell to store and execute SQL code. Stuxnet reduces the integrity level of objects to allow write actions. Stuxnet extracts and writes driver files that match the times of other legitimate files. Stuxnet decrypts resources that are loaded into memory and executed. Stuxnet can create registry keys to load driver files. Stuxnet propagates using the MS10-061 Print Spooler and MS08-067 Windows Server Service vulnerabilities. Stuxnet used WMI with an explorer.exe token to execute on a remote share. Stuxnet attempts to access network resources with a domain account’s credentials. Stuxnet can propagate via removable media using an autorun.inf file or the CVE-2010-2568 LNK vulnerability. Stuxnet infected WinCC machines via a hardcoded database server password. Stuxnet enumerates removable drives for infection. Stuxnet used a digitally signed driver with a compromised Realtek certificate. Stuxnet checks for specific operating systems on 32-bit machines, Registry keys, and dates for vulnerabilities, and will exit execution if the values are not met. Stuxnet collects system information including computer and domain names, OS version, and S7P paths. Stuxnet enumerates the currently running processes related to a variety of security products. Stuxnet uses a driver to scan for specific filesystem driver objects. Stuxnet schedules a network job to execute two minutes after host infection. Stuxnet uses HTTP to communicate with a command and control server. Stuxnet installs an RPC server for P2P communications. Stuxnet propagates to available network shares. Stuxnet enumerates user accounts of the domain. Stuxnet encrypts exfiltrated data via C2 with static 31-byte long XOR keys. Stuxnet sends compromised victim information via HTTP. Stuxnet injects an entire DLL into an existing, newly created, or preselected trusted process. Stuxnet uses an RPC server that contains a file dropping routine and support for payload version updates for P2P communications within a victim network. Stuxnet collects the time and date of a system when it is infected. Stuxnet uses an RPC server that contains a routine for file deletion and also removes itself from the system through a DLL export by deleting specific files. Stuxnet searches the Registry for indicators of security programs. Stuxnet uses a Windows rootkit to mask its binaries and other relevant files. Stuxnet has the ability to generate new C2 domains. Stuxnet can delete OLE Automation and SQL stored procedures used to store malicious payloads.
ref-9a160e23c7da35c0f4d7.title: Nicolas Falliere, Liam O Murchu, Eric Chien 2011, February W32.Stuxnet Dossier (Version 1.4) Retrieved November 17, 2024.

ref-baea562ccf87362fd1c5.text:
CASTLETAP can execute a C2 command to transfer files from victim machines.
CASTLETAP has the ability to spawn BusyBox command shell in victim environments.
THINCRUST can use Python scripts for command execution.
THINCRUST can use HTTP POST requests in C2 communications.
CASTLETAP can transfer files to compromised network devices.
CASTLETAP can filter and deobfuscate an XOR encrypted activation string in the payload of an ICMP echo request.
THINCRUST can use the Django python module "django.views.decorators.csrf” along with the decorator “csrf_exempt” within victim firewalls to disable cross-site request forgery protections.
THINCRUST can deobfuscate RSA encrypted C2 commands received through the DEVICEID cookie.
CASTLETAP can listen for a specialized ICMP packet for activation on compromised network devices.
THINCRUST can process RSA encryted C2 commands.
CASTLETAP can initiate a C2 connection over an SSL socket.
CASTLETAP has the ability to create a raw promiscuous socket to sniff network traffic.
CASTLETAP can receive a 9-byte XOR encrypted activation string in the payload of an ICMP echo request packet.
ref-baea562ccf87362fd1c5.title: Marvi, A. et al.. (2023, March 16). Fortinet Zero-Day and Custom Malware Used by Suspected Chinese Actor in Espionage Operation. Retrieved March 22, 2023.

ref-cf92338290010c363410.text: RGDoor encrypts files with XOR before sending them back to the C2 server. RGDoor uses HTTP for C2 communications. RGDoor decodes Base64 strings and decrypts strings using a custom XOR algorithm. RGDoor uploads and downloads files to and from the victim’s machine. RGDoor executes the whoami on the victim’s machine. RGDoor uses cmd.exe to execute commands on the victim’s machine.
ref-cf92338290010c363410.title: Falcone, R. (2018, January 25). OilRig uses RGDoor IIS Backdoor on Targets in the Middle East. Retrieved July 6, 2018.

ref-e4d916e2fe97c049be1e.text:
Keydnap uses HTTPS for command and control.
Keydnap uses the keychaindump project to read securityd memory.
Keydnap uses a Launch Agent to persist.
Keydnap uses Python for scripting to execute additional commands.
Keydnap puts a space after a false .jpg extension so that execution actually goes through the Terminal.app program.
Keydnap uses a copy of tor2web proxy for HTTPS communications.
Keydnap prompts the users for credentials.
ref-e4d916e2fe97c049be1e.title: Patrick Wardle. (2017, January 1). Mac Malware of 2016. Retrieved September 21, 2018.

ref-ec94a0a96d6440674c03.text:
Milan can query `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography MachineGuid` to retrieve the machine GUID.
Shark can query `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography MachineGuid` to retrieve the machine GUID.
Milan can establish persistence on a targeted host with scheduled tasks.
Shark can download additional files from its C2 via HTTP or DNS.
Shark can upload files to its C2.
Milan can use hardcoded domains as an input for domain generation algorithms.
Shark can use encrypted and encoded files for C2 configuration.
Shark can send DNS C2 communications using a unique domain generation algorithm.
Shark has the ability to use HTTP in C2 communications.
Milan can enumerate the targeted machine's name and GUID.
Shark can collect the GUID of a targeted machine.
Shark can use DNS in C2 communications.
Shark has the ability to use `CMD` to execute commands.
ref-ec94a0a96d6440674c03.title: Accenture. (2021, November 9). Who are latest targets of cyber group Lyceum?. Retrieved June 16, 2022.

ref-ed9fd713821239dc3ad8.text: SpeakUp can perform brute forcing using a pre-defined list of usernames and passwords in an attempt to log in to administrative panels. SpeakUp uses the arp -a command. SpeakUp uses Python scripts. SpeakUp uses cron tasks to ensure persistence. SpeakUp uses POST and GET requests over HTTP to communicate with its main C&C server. SpeakUp encodes C&C communication using Base64. SpeakUp encodes its second-stage payload with Base64. SpeakUp uses Perl scripts. SpeakUp attempts to exploit the following vulnerabilities in order to execute its malicious script: CVE-2012-0874, CVE-2010-1871, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2018-2894, CVE-2016-3088, JBoss AS 3/4/5/6, and the Hadoop YARN ResourceManager. SpeakUp uses the ifconfig -a command. SpeakUp deletes files to remove evidence on the machine. SpeakUp uses the whoami command. SpeakUp checks for availability of specific ports on servers. SpeakUp uses the cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep -c “cpu family” 2>&1 command to gather system information. SpeakUp downloads and executes additional files from a remote server.
ref-ed9fd713821239dc3ad8.title: Check Point Research. (2019, February 4). SpeakUp: A New Undetected Backdoor Linux Trojan. Retrieved April 17, 2019.

ref-f909d16decf204a6a5f2.text:
DUSTTRAP can retrieve and load additional payloads.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate Registry items.
DUSTPAN decrypts and executes an embedded payload.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate domain accounts.
DUSTTRAP can identify infected system log information.
DUSTTRAP can use `ping` to identify remote hosts within the victim network.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate local user accounts.
DUSTTRAP can execute commands via `cmd.exe`.
DUSTPAN decodes and decrypts embedded payloads.
DUSTTRAP can capture screenshots.
DUSTTRAP can remove network shares from infected systems.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate infected system network information.
DUSTPAN can inject its decrypted payload into another process.
DUSTPAN decrypts an embedded payload.
DUSTTRAP can identify and enumerate victim system network shares.
DUSTTRAP contains additional embedded DLLs and configuration files that are loaded into memory during execution.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate running processes.
DUSTTRAP reads the infected system's current time and writes it to a log file during execution.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate running application windows.
DUSTPAN is often disguised as a legitimate Windows binary such as `w3wp.exe` or `conn.exe`.
DUSTTRAP begins with an initial launcher that decrypts an AES-128-CFB encrypted file on disk and executes it in memory.
DUSTTRAP can gather data from infected systems.
DUSTTRAP compromises the `.text` section of a legitimate system DLL in `%windir%` to hold the contents of retrieved plug-ins.
DUSTTRAP restores the `.text` section of compromised DLLs after malicious code is loaded into memory and before the file is closed.
DUSTTRAP can identify victim environment Group Policy information.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate files and directories.
DUSTTRAP can delete infected system log information.
DUSTPAN can persist as a Windows Service in operations.
DUSTTRAP can perform keylogging operations.
DUSTTRAP can exfiltrate collected data over C2 channels.
DUSTTRAP can identify Active Directory information and related items.
DUSTTRAP deobfuscates embedded payloads.
DUSTTRAP decryption relies on the infected machine's `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGUID` value.
DUSTTRAP can identify security software.
DUSTTRAP reads the value of the infected system's `HKLM\SYSTEM\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGUID` value.
ref-f909d16decf204a6a5f2.title: Mike Stokkel et al. (2024, July 18). APT41 Has Arisen From the DUST. Retrieved September 16, 2024.
